statement_paragraphs: I am the counsel on record for the petitioner in WP No. 1234/2026.

facts.narrative: Accused induced the complainant to invest INR 10,00,000 in a fictitious real-estate scheme. Accused forged the allotment letter and has since absconded.

facts.impugned_order_summary: The Sessions Court rejected the appellant's application for stay on the recovery proceedings, holding that no prima facie case for stay was made out and that the balance of convenience lay with the respondent revenue authority.
questions_of_law: Whether the Sessions Court erred in declining stay despite the demand exceeding the assessed liability by 38%.
Whether the balance of convenience requires deposit of the disputed component pending appeal.
facts.grounds_brief: 1. The Sessions Court overlooked the appellant's documented payment of the undisputed component of the demand. 2. The court mis-read Annexure D-2 (statutory acknowledgement). 3. The court applied the wrong test for stay under CPC Order XLI Rule 5 by demanding security for the entire demand rather than the disputed portion. 4. No reasoned finding was recorded on irreparable injury despite the appellant placing on record bank-statement evidence of liquidity strain.
facts.interim_relief_sought: Stay of recovery proceedings pending hearing of this appeal, conditional on deposit of the undisputed component already paid.
facts.record_references: Impugned order at pp. 14-19 of paper-book; Annexure D-2 at p. 47; bank statements at pp. 81-93.

The parties have since entered into a written compromise dated 2026-02-10 under which the petitioner has refunded the disputed amount with interest.
facts.grounds_for_quashing: The dispute is predominantly civil and commercial in nature; the parties have entered into a written compromise; continuation of proceedings would be an abuse of the process of court.

preliminary_objections: The plaint is barred by limitation under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
The suit is undervalued for the purpose of pecuniary jurisdiction.
facts.paragraph_wise_reply: Para 1 is a matter of record. Para 2 is admitted insofar as the agreement to sell dated 2024-05-01 is concerned. Para 3 is denied; the plaintiff failed to tender the balance consideration within the time stipulated. Para 4 is denied for want of knowledge. Paras 5 to 8 are denied save and except as specifically admitted herein.
facts.limitation_defence: The cause of action accrued on 2024-12-01 when the plaintiff defaulted; the suit filed on 2026-04-15 is beyond the three-year limitation period.
documents_relied: Bank statements showing non-receipt of balance consideration

facts.main_petition_summary: The petitioner challenges Notification No. 12/2025 dated 2025-11-30 on the ground that it violates Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
facts.paragraph_wise_response: The contents of paras 1 to 3 are matters of record. Para 4 is denied. The notification was issued after due consultation with the stakeholder ministries and an inter-ministerial review committee, and is a valid exercise of statutory power conferred under s.5 of the parent Act. Paras 5 and 6 are denied. The remaining paras are denied save to the extent expressly admitted.
additional_facts_pleaded: The respondent has placed on record the inter-ministerial consultation file by way of separate affidavit.
The petitioner has suppressed the fact that representations were entertained by the respondent on 2026-01-10 and 2026-02-15.
facts.preliminary_submissions: The writ petition is liable to be dismissed at the threshold for suppression of material facts and for want of cause of action.
facts.relief_sought_against_petition: Dismiss the writ petition with costs.

facts.grounds_for_quashing: The petitioner and the aggrieved person have arrived at a comprehensive settlement of their matrimonial disputes, including a mutually-acceptable visitation schedule for the minor child. Continuation of the magistrate proceedings would be an abuse of process and is no longer in the interest of either party or the child.

facts.impugned_order_summary: Bombay High Court order dated 12 March 2026 in Writ Petition No. 4523/2025 dismissing the petitioner's challenge to the demolition notice issued by the respondent under Section 53 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966.
questions_of_law: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to interfere with a demolition notice issued without compliance with the natural-justice requirements laid down in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) 3 SCC 545.
Whether the proviso to Section 53 mandates a personal hearing before demolition can be ordered.
facts.grounds_brief: The High Court overlooked binding precedent on the natural-justice requirement before demolition. The order proceeds on the assumption that a written show-cause notice substitutes for the right to a personal hearing, which is contrary to Olga Tellis and the line of cases following it. The petition raises a substantial question of law of general public importance fit for adjudication under Article 136.
facts.interim_relief_sought: Stay of demolition pending disposal of the SLP.

facts.impugned_order_summary: Bombay High Court Division Bench judgment dated 4 February 2026 in First Appeal No. 312/2024 reversing the trial court's decree of specific performance and remanding the matter for fresh consideration on quantum of damages. The High Court certified the matter as fit for appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 133.
facts.substantial_question: Whether a remand limited to quantum amounts to a reversal on liability for the purposes of Section 100 CPC and whether such a partial remand can be made without first deciding the issue of breach.
facts.grounds_brief: The High Court's remand exceeds the scope permitted under Order XLI Rule 23A CPC. The substantial question of law concerns the boundary between a reversal on liability (which must be final) and a remand on quantum. The Supreme Court's settled position in Municipal Corporation, Hyderabad v. Sunder Singh Naharh (2008) 8 SCC 42 is at variance with the impugned approach.

facts.error_apparent_on_face_of_record: The judgment proceeds on the recorded finding that the petitioner did not raise the limitation defence before the High Court. That finding is contrary to the record — paragraph 17 of the High Court order expressly notes the limitation argument and rejects it on merits. The mistake is a self-evident error apparent on the face of the record within the narrow band recognised in Northern India Caterers v. Lt. Governor of Delhi (1980) 2 SCC 167.
facts.grounds_brief: Review jurisdiction under Article 137 is narrow; the petitioner does not seek a rehearing on merits. The petition is confined to the factual mistake that the limitation point was not raised — a mistake apparent from paragraph 17 of the impugned High Court order which is itself part of the record before this Hon'ble Court.

facts.senior_advocate_name: Sh. R. K. Anand, Senior Advocate
facts.grounds_brief: Per Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) 4 SCC 388, the curative jurisdiction is invoked only when (a) there has been a violation of the principles of natural justice or (b) where the judge who passed the order failed to disclose facts giving rise to apprehension of bias. The present petition is grounded on (a) — the impugned order was passed without notice to the petitioner on the additional submission filed by the respondent on 11 August 2025.
facts.natural_justice_violation: The respondent's note of 11 August 2025 was placed on record after oral arguments concluded and before the judgment was reserved. The petitioner had no opportunity to respond. The judgment expressly relies on paragraphs 4 and 7 of that note for its reasoning on the licence cancellation.

facts.grounds_for_transfer: The petitioner is a single mother residing with her infant daughter in New Delhi. Travel to Ghaziabad for each hearing requires a six-hour round trip and overnight childcare arrangements that the petitioner cannot afford. The respondent ordinarily works in Delhi NCR and would not be inconvenienced by transfer.
facts.convenience_reasons: Petitioner's permanent residence is in Saket; child is enrolled in a Delhi school; petitioner is the sole caregiver.
facts.safety_or_threat_reasons: Two FIRs registered against the respondent under Section 498A IPC (Ghaziabad) and Section 354 BNS (Saket). Petitioner has been advised by counsel against attending hearings in Ghaziabad without protection.

facts.contemnor_name: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority and its Chief Executive Officer Sh. R. K. Sinha
facts.underlying_order_summary: Allahabad High Court order dated 4 November 2025 in Writ Petition No. 9876/2024 directing the respondent authority to release the petitioner's possession of Plot No. 14, Sector Beta-II within sixty days and pay arrears of compensation as quantified in paragraph 23 of the order.
facts.breach_facts: The sixty-day period expired on 3 January 2026. The respondent has neither restored possession nor paid the quantified compensation. Reminders dated 8 January 2026 and 22 February 2026 have been ignored. The breach is wilful — the respondent's standing counsel has confirmed in writing that the order will not be complied with pending an internal review which has no statutory basis.
facts.relief_sought: Adjudge and punish the contemnor for civil contempt under Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; direct immediate compliance with the order dated 4 November 2025.

facts.main_proceeding_summary: Writ petition pending before the Bombay High Court challenging the demand notice dated 5 March 2026 for INR 47,82,00,000 raised under Section 156 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 pursuant to a reassessment order under Section 147. The petition pleads that the reassessment is barred by limitation under Section 149.
facts.prima_facie_case: The reassessment notice was issued on 30 March 2025 — beyond the three-year ordinary limit under Section 149(1)(a). The Revenue's reliance on the extended ten-year limit under Section 149(1)(b) requires escaped income exceeding INR 50 lakh, which the impugned notice does not establish on its face. The petitioner has demonstrable arguable grounds.
facts.balance_of_convenience: Recovery of INR 47.82 crores from the petitioner's working capital would impair its production and supply commitments to government health agencies. The Revenue, by contrast, will not be prejudiced by stay during the pendency of a writ that is set down for final hearing within sixty days.
facts.irreparable_injury: Coercive recovery would force the petitioner into a default on its ongoing supply contracts, including price-controlled pharmaceutical contracts with state procurement agencies. Reputational and contractual injury cannot be undone by a later refund.
facts.undertaking_offered: The petitioner undertakes to deposit twenty per cent of the disputed demand within four weeks as a condition of stay, without prejudice to its rights.

facts.diligence_explanation: The applicant retained counsel within seven days of the impugned High Court order on 12 January 2026 and instructed counsel to brief Senior Advocate for the SLP. The drafting and certification work resumed immediately upon the applicant's clearance to travel on 1 March 2026; the SLP was finalised and filed on 19 March 2026 — within the shortest practicable window post-recovery.

facts.case_title: Sunrise Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Mumbai-1
questions_of_law: Whether a reassessment notice under Section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 issued beyond the three-year limit under Section 149(1)(a) can be sustained in the absence of a finding that the escaped income exceeds INR 50 lakh as required by Section 149(1)(b).
Whether the High Court was correct in declining to interfere with the demand notice when the underlying reassessment order is itself under challenge on limitation grounds.
facts.case_summary: The petitioner is a listed pharmaceutical company. For Assessment Year 2018-19 the original assessment was completed on 28 December 2020 under Section 143(3). On 30 March 2025 the Revenue issued a reassessment notice under Section 148 alleging escapement of income. The reassessment order followed on 28 February 2026 raising a demand of INR 47.82 crores. The petitioner challenged the reassessment before the Bombay High Court on limitation and jurisdictional grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on 22 February 2026, leading to the present SLP.
chronology: 2020-12-28: Original assessment for AY 2018-19 completed under Section 143(3).
2025-03-30: Reassessment notice issued under Section 148 for AY 2018-19.
2025-04-25: Petitioner's reply to the reassessment notice filed.
2026-02-28: Reassessment order under Section 147 raising demand of INR 47.82 crores.
2026-03-05: Demand notice under Section 156 served on the petitioner.
2026-03-08: Writ petition WP No. 8472 of 2025 filed before the Bombay High Court.
2026-02-22: Bombay High Court order dismissing the writ petition (impugned).
2026-04-14: Present SLP filed before this Hon'ble Court.
